content: The study was significantly underpowered to reliably detect differences in energy expenditure. The reported 7% increase in total energy expenditure per kilogram of body weight was deemed not significant by the authors, and no p-value was provided. For further details, refer to supplementary information (63). The median control group risk across studies is detailed in the footnotes, and the corresponding risk (with its 95% confidence interval) is based on the assumed risk in the comparison group and the relative effect of the intervention (and its 95% CI). The GRADE Working Group classifies evidence quality as follows: High quality: High confidence that the true effect is close to the estimated effect. Moderate quality: Moderate confidence in the effect estimate, with a possibility of substantial differences. Low quality: Limited confidence in the effect estimate, with a high likelihood of substantial differences. Very low quality: Very little confidence in the effect estimate, with the true effect likely to differ substantially. One study in India randomized 103 patients aged over 12 years with tuberculosis (TB) to receive either monthly ration packs or nutritional advice alone. Another study in India randomized 100 adults with TB to receive either a daily locally appropriate food supplement or nutritional advice alone. The supplement consisted of sweet balls providing 6 grams of protein and 600 kcal per day. One study adequately concealed allocation, while another did not. Both studies were open-label. These studies were conducted exclusively in India, where nutritional status and food availability may differ significantly from other settings, limiting the generalizability of the findings. The trials were severely underpowered to detect clinically meaningful effects, with an optimal sample size estimated at 2,000 participants. For example, Martins (2009) did not report any deaths after randomization. Another trial in Timor-Leste randomized 270 adults with TB to receive either a daily hot meal or nutritional advice alone. One study found a statistically significant benefit of supplementation, while the other did not. These two studies, conducted in Timor-Leste and India, highlight the challenges of generalizing results to other settings or subpopulations. One study in Singapore compared high-energy nutritional supplements (approximately 900 kcal) plus nutritional advice versus nutritional advice alone in 36 adults. Data from these studies appeared highly skewed and could not be pooled. A study in Tanzania randomized 865 adults with TB and HIV co-infection to receive six high-energy protein biscuits or one. The small observed benefit was not statistically significant. Another study included only HIV-positive patients and showed a trend toward benefit, but this did not reach statistical significance. Weight gain with supplementation was statistically significant in three studies. For details of the studies included in the review, see reference (27). The WHO guideline on nutritional care and support for TB patients emphasizes the importance of nutritional assessment and counseling. People with active TB are often underweight and have experienced weight loss by the time of diagnosis. Low BMI is associated with increased mortality, necessitating nutrition screening and assessment to determine appropriate interventions. Management of Severe Acute Malnutrition in Adults with TB The quality of evidence is very low. In the absence of direct evidence that treating severe acute malnutrition in TB patients improves TB outcomes, the panel recommends treating these patients similarly to severely malnourished individuals without TB, following established standards of care. Benefits are likely, as severe acute malnutrition increases mortality risk in TB patients. Therapeutic food products for children, such as F-100 or ready-to-use therapeutic foods, may be used for adults in settings where appropriate products for adults are unavailable. Resource implications for TB programs are considered moderate to high, and linking TB services with nutrition programs is recommended. Management of Moderate Undernutrition in Adults with TB The quality of evidence is low. Macronutrient supplementation likely improves weight gain during the intensive phase of TB treatment (moderate-quality evidence). However, no clear benefits of supplementation on TB treatment outcomes have been demonstrated. Locally available nutrient-rich or fortified foods may not always be accessible, and there are no established recommendations for managing moderate undernutrition in various age groups. Resource implications for TB programs are high, and integration with other health services or nutrition programs is recommended. Micronutrient Supplementation in TB Patients The quality of evidence is very low. While low serum levels of essential micronutrients are common in TB patients, randomized trials have not shown significant clinical benefits of micronutrient supplementation on TB treatment outcomes. Plasma levels of certain vitamins and minerals normalize by the end of treatment, regardless of supplementation. Supplementation is unlikely to be harmful but may increase financial burdens unless provided free of charge. Resource implications for programs are considered low. Micronutrient Supplementation in Pregnant and Lactating Women with TB The quality of evidence is very low. Increased physiological requirements during pregnancy and lactation, combined with the likelihood of undernutrition, justify micronutrient supplementation. Trials in pregnant women with HIV have shown benefits of multiple micronutrient supplementation on maternal and infant outcomes. Calcium supplementation is recommended to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia. Resource implications for TB programs are low, and coordination with antenatal services is required. Nutritional Care for Household Contacts of TB Patients The quality of evidence is very low. Undernourished individuals, particularly young children under five years of age, are at higher risk of progressing from latent to active TB. Nutritional screening and assessment can identify high-risk contacts who require evaluation for active and latent TB. Resource implications for TB screening programs are considered low.
